fatal_flaws.claim: §5.4 Layer 3: the zod schema's regexes and length caps are presented as structural guarantees — `Hex = z.string().regex(/^#[0-9a-f]{6}$/)`, `Plain = z.string().max(600).regex(/^[^<>{}\\]*$/)`, `Href` path regexes, `.max(9)/.max(14)/.max(36)` — making T1/T4 "structurally impossible rather than filtered."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Anthropic structured outputs support only a narrow JSON Schema subset: basic types, `enum`, `const`, `anyOf`, `allOf`, `$ref`/`$def`, named string *formats* (date-time, email, uri, uuid, …) and `additionalProperties: false`. Explicitly NOT supported: string constraints (`minLength`, `maxLength`), numerical constraints, complex array constraints, recursive schemas. `pattern` is not in the supported set at all. The Python and TypeScript SDKs silently strip unsupported constraints from the schema sent to the API and validate them client-side. So none of these regexes or caps constrain decoding — the model is free to emit `#FFAA00` (the regex is lowercase-only; models emit uppercase hex constantly), a 900-character headline, or 40 pages. The constraint then fires as a client-side zod failure inside `messages.parse()`, `parsed_output` comes back null, and the €1–3 call is already paid for. The design has converted its main XSS control into an expensive, high-frequency reliability failure — and the true XSS defense is only Layers 4–6 (renderer + HTMLRewriter + CSP), which is not what §5.1 claims.
fatal_flaws.correction: Move every value constraint out of the schema and into post-parse normalisation: accept `z.string()` for text and `z.string()` for colour, then in code lowercase/validate the hex (falling back to the industry preset on mismatch), truncate text to 600 chars, and slice arrays to their caps. Use `enum`/`const` — which ARE enforced — for everything that can be closed (block `type`, `locale`, `page.key`, `font`, anchor hrefs). Never let a schema-validation failure be the thing that fails a paid job; log it, repair it, and let Layers 4–6 be the actual security boundary (which they already are).

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.5: "Anonymous first generation: `output_config: { effort: "medium" }`, `max_tokens: 32000`, streaming, one call" — while §2.1's own cost table budgets "Output + thinking (typical) 45 k" and §5.4's schema permits `pages` up to 36 (6 pages × 6 locales) each with up to 14 blocks, plus 2 blog posts and legal text.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: This is internally contradictory and guarantees failure on the happy path. The document's own typical-case estimate (45k output tokens) is 40% above the configured `max_tokens` of 32000. Thinking tokens count against `max_tokens` and bill as output, so adaptive thinking eats the budget before the JSON starts. When the cap is hit the response returns `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` with truncated JSON — structured outputs explicitly warn that output may be incomplete in this case — so `messages.parse()` yields no valid `parsed_output`. You pay full price for ~32k output tokens and get nothing. Separately, 36 locale-page objects of real marketing copy is not a 32k-token document under any encoding.
fatal_flaws.correction: Either raise `max_tokens` to 64000–128000 for the single call (which forces streaming and roughly doubles the worst-case per-generation cost the funnel is sized against — re-derive the $500/day cap from that number), or split generation: one call for the source-locale site tree, then per-locale translation calls that reuse a cached prefix. The second is cheaper, cache-friendlier, degrades gracefully, and makes "trivially extensible to more languages" actually true. Whichever you pick, assert `stop_reason !== "max_tokens"` before charging the reservation.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.5: "Hard `AbortController` timeout (180 s)" on the single Anthropic generation call.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: A single `claude-opus-5` call producing 30–60k output tokens with adaptive thinking takes many minutes, not 180 seconds. The 180 s abort will fire on the majority of successful generations, after the tokens have already been generated and billed. Worse, it fires inside a Queue consumer: the consumer throws, Cloudflare retries the message (Queues retry by default), and a second full-price generation starts — while `BudgetDO.settle()` never runs, so the reservation is force-settled at estimate by the 10-minute alarm and `gens` is never decremented. You get 2–4× the spend per job and a budget counter that only ever ratchets up. Nothing in the design bounds Queue-level retries; `generation_jobs.attempts <= 2` is an application counter the Queue does not consult. Note the platform ceiling that actually matters here is the Queue consumer duration limit of 15 minutes, not 180 s.
fatal_flaws.correction: Set the abort to ~12 minutes (under the 15-minute Queue consumer limit), set `max_retries: 1` on the queue consumer, make the job row the retry authority (`INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on `job_id` before dispatch, ack the message on any terminal outcome including failure), and have `settle()` decrement `gens` as well as release `reservedMicro` on abort/failure. Also configure `limits.cpu_ms` explicitly — the default consumer CPU cap is 30 s and the media path re-encodes 12 images into AVIF, which Cloudflare documents as an order of magnitude slower than other encodes.

fatal_flaws.why_wrong: This puts fully attacker-influenced, ungated generated HTML on the single origin that holds every authenticated cookie — `__Host-aib_sess`, `__Host-aib_ctx`, `__Host-aib_anon`. The HTMLRewriter output gate (§5.6) runs "before a version is written to `content_blobs` / published" — a preview of an unclaimed draft is by definition pre-publish, so the gate has not run. Any renderer bug becomes same-origin script execution on the dashboard, and `__Host-` prefixes do nothing about same-origin XSS — they only stop cross-subdomain cookie shadowing. The design contradicts itself twice: §8.2's app CSP allowlists `frame-src https://preview.mijnsaas.com` (a separate origin that §3.2 never creates), and §5.8 item 2 states the preview iframe must be a different origin with `sandbox` and no `allow-same-origin`.
fatal_flaws.correction: Serve every preview from a dedicated cookieless origin — `preview.mijnsaas.com` (or better, the separate tenant domain floated in §5.8 item 3) — with the §5.7 `default-src 'none'` CSP, `X-Robots-Tag: noindex`, and the HTMLRewriter gate applied on the preview path too, not only at publish. The app embeds it in a sandboxed iframe without `allow-same-origin`. Make "no generated HTML is ever served from the cookie origin" an invariant with a test, alongside the membership-join invariant.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.3 allowlist includes `image/heic`, and §4.2 makes re-encoding through `env.IMAGES` mandatory for every image ("RE-ENCODE (mandatory)", "Re-encoding is the single highest-value control here").
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Cloudflare Images supports PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG and AVIF as input formats — **HEIC ingestion is Enterprise-plan only**. HEIC/HEIF is the iPhone camera default, and the stated target audience is small local business owners uploading photos from a phone. On any non-Enterprise Images plan, every HEIC upload passes the magic-byte sniff (`ftyp`/`heic`), then fails the mandatory re-encode, and the design's own rule is "sniffed type must EQUAL the declared type… No 'close enough'" with failure → `status='failed'`. The most common upload in the product's most common flow is a hard error. Two further unbudgeted constraints in the same paragraph: the Images binding's `.input()` maximum is 20 MB (the design's 15 MB image cap survives, but ProRAW/HEIF bursts do not), and Images is billed at $0.50 per 1,000 unique transformations with only 5,000 free per month — the design's 2400px master plus 400/800/1600 in both WebP and AVIF is ~7 billable transformations per image, so the free tier is exhausted at roughly 60 sites.
fatal_flaws.correction: Either drop HEIC from the allowlist and do the HEIC→JPEG conversion client-side (browsers on iOS will hand you JPEG if the file input is given `accept="image/jpeg,image/png,image/webp"`, and `canvas.toBlob()` covers the rest), or price Images Enterprise before committing to the pipeline. Cut the variant matrix — WebP-only at 400/800/1600 plus the master is 4 transformations, and AVIF's marginal Lighthouse gain does not justify doubling both the bill and the CPU (Cloudflare documents AVIF encoding as an order of magnitude slower). Put the Images and Stream line items in §2.1 alongside the Anthropic number.

fatal_flaws.claim: §8.5 + §10 delta 2: single D1 database created with `jurisdiction: eu`, holding all 31 tables for all tenants, with every dashboard query as `JOIN memberships m ON m.org_id = ? AND m.user_id = ?`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: A D1 database is capped at 10 GB and Cloudflare states the limit "cannot be further increased" — D1 is explicitly designed for horizontal scale-out across multiple smaller databases (per-tenant/per-entity). The design never mentions the cap or a sharding strategy. At 10,000 tenants with `leads` on 12-month retention, `site_versions`, `media_assets`, `audit_log` on 12 months, `stripe_events` on 24 months, `sessions`, `anon_sessions` and `abuse_events`, 10 GB is reachable within a couple of years — and there is no online path out, because the entire identity/billing/quota model assumes cross-tenant single-database joins. This compounds with a genuine one-way door: a D1 jurisdiction "can only be set on database creation and cannot be added or updated after the database exists." You cannot resize, and you cannot migrate a non-`eu` database into `eu`.
fatal_flaws.correction: Decide the shard key now, before the first `wrangler d1 create`. Keep one small control-plane DB (`users`, `organisations`, `memberships`, `sessions`, `subscriptions`, `sites` → `shard_id`) and put per-site heavy data (`leads`, `site_versions`, `media_assets`, `content`) in numbered shard DBs, each created with `--jurisdiction=eu`. Route via a shard-lookup in the control plane. Even if you launch with one shard, having the `shard_id` column and the routing indirection from migration 0001 is the difference between a config change and a rewrite. Add a size alarm at 6 GB.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.2 presign code: `new Request(\`https://${ACCOUNT}.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/aibuilder-quarantine/${key}\`, …)` combined with §10 delta 2's "set `jurisdiction = \"eu\"` on all buckets."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Jurisdictional buckets are reachable only through their jurisdiction-specific S3 endpoint. For the EU jurisdiction that is `https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` — the `.eu.` label is mandatory. Cloudflare states that jurisdictional buckets "can only be accessed via the corresponding jurisdictional endpoint" and that from a jurisdiction endpoint you cannot reach resources outside it. Every presigned URL the design issues will be signed for a host that does not contain the bucket, and every browser PUT fails. Because the signature covers the host, this is not fixable by rewriting the URL after signing.
fatal_flaws.correction: Sign against `https://${ACCOUNT}.eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/aibuilder-quarantine/${key}`, and put the endpoint host in config keyed to the jurisdiction rather than hardcoding it. Also note this bites the R2 CORS configuration (must be set on the EU-jurisdiction bucket via the same endpoint) and Logpush, which Cloudflare documents as not interacting with jurisdiction-assigned R2 resources — so the "AI transcripts in R2 / 90-day lifecycle" audit trail needs an S3-endpoint Logpush job, not the default one.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.6: "Same widget on tenant lead forms" + "Turnstile is free at unlimited volume on the standard plan", and pre-clearance recommended to avoid a double challenge.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Three hard limits the design does not account for, all of which bite in Phase 3 (custom domains): (1) a Turnstile widget on the free plan allows a maximum of **10 hostnames**; Enterprise raises it to 200. Adding `mijnsaas.com` covers all `<slug>.mijnsaas.com` subdomains, so the slug sites are fine — but 10,000 tenants on their own custom domains cannot be covered by any per-widget hostname list. (2) "Any Hostname" is **Enterprise only**. (3) Pre-clearance `cf_clearance` cookies are only accepted on domains that are "registered as zones in your Cloudflare account" and are orange-clouded — Cloudflare for SaaS custom hostnames are not zones in your account, so pre-clearance simply does not apply there. So the lead-form protection story works on `<slug>.mijnsaas.com` and collapses the moment a customer attaches their own domain, which is the headline Phase 3 feature. Separately, free accounts are capped at 20 widgets per account, so "one widget per tenant" is not an escape hatch either.
fatal_flaws.correction: Do not use Turnstile on tenant lead forms at custom domains. Protect `POST /v1/leads/:site_id` with the per-tenant D1 origin allowlist you already build in §8.3, a Workers rate-limit binding keyed on site_id + hashed IP, a proof-of-work or timing/honeypot check, and server-side spam scoring — then price Turnstile Enterprise only if abuse actually materialises. Fix the `leads.turnstile_ok` column's meaning accordingly rather than leaving a column that is always 0 on the surface that matters.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.7 tenant CSP (`script-src 'sha256-<the one tiny script>'; connect-src 'self' https://api.mijnsaas.com`) alongside §9: "Analytics: Cloudflare Web Analytics (cookieless) … never a third-party tag on a tenant page — it would blow both the CSP and the Lighthouse score."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Cloudflare Web Analytics *is* a third-party tag: the beacon loads from `https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js`, and Cloudflare's own CSP guidance says you must add `script-src static.cloudflareinsights.com; connect-src cloudflareinsights.com`. Under the §5.7 policy the beacon script is blocked outright. Automatic injection makes it worse — the injected tag carries no hash and no nonce, so it is blocked with no way to allowlist it short of naming the host. The two sections directly contradict each other, and as written you ship tenant sites with analytics that silently never fire. Second CSP bug in the same block: `style-src 'sha256-…'` permits the hashed inline `<style>` element but does **not** permit `style="…"` attributes — those need `'unsafe-hashes'`. "Theme applied as CSS custom properties" and the "sticky WhatsApp chat button in site colors" will be silently unstyled if any of that lands in an inline style attribute, which is the natural way to emit a per-tenant `--primary`.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add `https://static.cloudflareinsights.com` to `script-src` and `https://cloudflareinsights.com` to `connect-src` on tenant sites (proxied sites POST to same-origin `/cdn-cgi/rum`, which `'self'` already covers), or drop the beacon entirely and use Analytics Engine written server-side from `worker-sites` — which is what "never a third-party tag" actually implies and costs zero client bytes. Emit every theme value inside the hashed `<style>` block as `:root{--primary:#…}` and forbid `style=` attributes in the renderer, or add `'unsafe-hashes'` and hash each attribute value.

fatal_flaws.claim: §1 trust-boundary diagram places `DOs` inside the `D1 (eu) R2 media (eu) … DOs` row, and §8.5 claims EU residency; QuotaDO is keyed on `sha256(nfkc(business_name)+postal_code)`, normalised email, E.164 phone and hashed IP.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Durable Objects are not EU-resident by default. A DO created with `env.NS.idFromName(x)` is placed near the first requester, anywhere in the world. Restricting them requires an explicit jurisdictional subnamespace — `env.MY_DO.jurisdiction("eu").idFromName(name)` — and Cloudflare notes the same name yields a *different* ID in a jurisdictional subnamespace. The design's DO sketch never does this. The QuotaDO's SQLite storage holds normalised emails, E.164 phone numbers and business-identity hashes; the BudgetDO holds job IDs. That is personal data persisted outside the EU while the privacy policy says otherwise — a documentation-vs-implementation gap that a DPA review will catch.
fatal_flaws.correction: Create every DO through `env.QUOTA_DO.jurisdiction("eu")` / `env.BUDGET_DO.jurisdiction("eu")` from the first line of code — retrofitting it later changes every DO ID and silently resets every quota counter, so this is effectively a one-way door too. Better still, do not store raw email/phone in the DO at all: key on `HMAC(IP_SALT, normalised_value)` so the DO holds only opaque 32-byte keys.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.4: 3 generations per IP / 24 h, 10 per IPv4 /24 (or IPv6 /48) / 24 h, enforced by QuotaDO; "Datacenter/VPS ASNs, Tor exits → 0 free generations".
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The target audience is small local businesses in Europe, and the onboarding flow is a mobile-first full-screen modal — so a large fraction of legitimate traffic arrives over mobile carrier CGNAT. European MNOs routinely put tens of thousands of subscribers behind a handful of IPv4 addresses inside one /24. A 10-per-/24-per-day cap means the eleventh Vodafone NL customer to try your product on a given day is refused, with no signal distinguishing them from a bot. The IPv6 /48 limit is the opposite error: many residential ISPs delegate a /48 or /56 *per subscriber*, so /48 aggregation is close to per-household — fine — but mobile IPv6 often delegates /64 from shared /48 pools, putting you back in the same trap. This is the design's own failure mode from §2.4's degradation table ("a bot outage becomes a customer outage") reintroduced one row above it.
fatal_flaws.correction: Do not hard-block on IP-derived dimensions. Use them to *escalate*: over the /24 threshold, move the session into the "confirm email before generation" mode that §2.4 already defines for 70–85% budget utilisation. That preserves the abuse economics (a bot farm now needs a working inbox per generation) while costing a real baker 20 seconds. Keep hard blocks for the datacenter/Tor ASN case only, where the false-positive rate genuinely is near zero.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7: `return new Response("bad signature", { status: 400 })` with the comment `// 400 = never retried, correct`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Stripe retries on **any** non-2xx status. Stripe's docs state that when your endpoint replies with a non-2xx code, Stripe retries the event with a new signature and timestamp, continuing for up to 3 days with exponential backoff in live mode. There is no 4xx carve-out. So a rotated-secret misconfiguration, a body-parsing regression, or a proxy that mangles the raw body produces three days of retries and a webhook endpoint Stripe may auto-disable — not the clean drop the comment assumes. The stated rationale for choosing 400 is simply false.
fatal_flaws.correction: 400 is still the right status for an unverifiable signature (you must not 200 something you cannot authenticate), but document it correctly and add the operational consequence: alert on `webhook_endpoint` delivery-failure metrics, and make the raw-body read the first thing the handler does with no middleware ahead of it. Reserve 200-with-log for the one case where you *do* want retries to stop: a validly-signed event you have decided not to process.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7 idempotency: `INSERT … ON CONFLICT(stripe_event_id) DO UPDATE SET attempts = attempts+1, status='processing' WHERE stripe_events.status <> 'processed' RETURNING attempts;` → "No row returned ⇒ already processed ⇒ 200 immediately".
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: This is correct against *sequential* redelivery and wrong against *concurrent* redelivery. Stripe can deliver the same event twice with overlapping requests, and D1 has no interactive transactions or `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`. Two concurrent invocations both find `status <> 'processed'`, both get a row back, and both proceed to process. For the subscription path the design's own "re-read from the Stripe API and persist current state" mechanism makes the double-write idempotent, so this is survivable there — but any non-idempotent handler added later (issuing a credit, sending a provisioning call, incrementing a counter) will double-fire, and the design gives no rule preventing that. The claim that "replay of a captured body is therefore a no-op" is only true because of the re-read, not because of this SQL.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add a claim token to the guard: `… DO UPDATE SET status='processing', attempts=attempts+1, claimed_by=?, claimed_at=? WHERE stripe_events.status='pending' OR (stripe_events.status='processing' AND stripe_events.claimed_at < ?stale)` and require `meta.changes === 1` plus `claimed_by` matching your invocation id before doing any work — the same atomic-consume pattern the design already applies correctly to `site_claim_tokens` and `auth_tokens`. Then write the rule down: every webhook handler must be a pure function of re-read Stripe state.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.3: "Operator instructions added later in the conversation go in a mid-conversation system message (`{role: "system", …}` appended to `messages[]`) — supported on Opus 5, and it is the injection-safe operator channel that also preserves your cache prefix."
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The mechanism is real and correctly attributed to Opus 5 — this part of the design is right, and I want to be clear it is not an error. But the placement rules are omitted and they are strict enough to break naive code: a mid-conversation system message must follow a `user` message (or an `assistant` message ending in server-tool use), and must be either the last entry in `messages` or be followed by an `assistant` turn — it cannot be `messages[0]`. The design's §5.4 request has exactly two message entries (cached industry preset, then `<business_input>`), so any operator message appended after the untrusted block is legal, but a future refactor that puts it first will 400.
fatal_flaws.correction: Note the constraint next to the code: the untrusted `<business_input nonce=…>` user message must come before the operator system message, never after. That ordering is also the one you want for injection resistance and for cache-prefix stability, so it costs nothing to state explicitly.

fatal_flaws.why_wrong: HSTS preload submission requires the header to be served from the **apex** (`https://mijnsaas.com`) with `includeSubDomains` and `preload`, and requires the apex to redirect HTTP→HTTPS on the same host. The design deliberately puts nothing on the apex (marketing on `www`, app on `app`), so as specified the domain cannot be preloaded. This also collides with §5.8 item 3: preloading the apex with `includeSubDomains` and then adding `mijnsaas.com` to the Public Suffix List are two separate, slow-to-reverse one-way doors being proposed for the same name.
fatal_flaws.correction: Serve the apex (a 301 to `www` is enough) with the HSTS header if you want preload. And pick one of PSL-vs-preload deliberately — the cleanest resolution is the option §5.8 already floats: put tenant sites on a *separate registrable domain* (`mijnsaas.site`), which gives you the cookie/storage isolation instantly, removes the PSL dependency entirely, and — critically — stops one phishing tenant from getting `mijnsaas.com` onto Google Safe Browsing and taking every other tenant down with it.

fatal_flaws.claim: §6.3 passkeys: `rpID = app.mijnsaas.com`, and §5.8 item 3: "submit `mijnsaas.com` to the Public Suffix List".
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: These interact in a way the document does not notice. WebAuthn's rpID must be a registrable-domain suffix of the origin, and "registrable domain" is computed from the Public Suffix List. If `mijnsaas.com` is ever added to the PSL, `app.mijnsaas.com` becomes its own registrable domain — `rpID = app.mijnsaas.com` keeps working, but `rpID = mijnsaas.com` becomes invalid and **every passkey registered under it is permanently unusable**, with no migration path (you cannot re-key a credential to a different RP ID). The design happens to pick the safe value, but nothing records *why*, so the first person who "simplifies" the rpID to the apex creates an unrecoverable auth outage.
fatal_flaws.correction: Write the constraint into the code as a comment and a test: `rpID` is `app.mijnsaas.com` and may never be broadened to the apex, because of the PSL plan. Same for cookies — the `__Host-` prefix already forbids `Domain`, which is what makes the app PSL-safe; keep it that way.

fatal_flaws.claim: §8.4: "Cloudflare Secrets Store (account-level, RBAC, audit) via `secrets_store_secrets` bindings" as the primary secrets mechanism, with separate keys per environment.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Secrets Store is in open beta, and there can be **only one store per account** with a cap of 100 production secrets and 1024 bytes per secret. "One store per account" means dev/staging/prod secrets share a store and are separated by naming convention plus RBAC, not by a hard boundary — which is weaker than the design's framing implies. Betting the whole capability-separation story on an open-beta product for a Phase 1 deliverable is a schedule risk the doc does not price.
fatal_flaws.correction: The design is otherwise right that per-Worker bindings are the real capability boundary — keep the four-Worker split, but make the secret source pluggable: `await env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.get?.() ?? env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` so `wrangler secret put` works as the fallback and in local dev. Use separate Cloudflare accounts (not just separate secret names) for prod vs. non-prod if the environment boundary actually matters.

fatal_flaws.why_wrong: FLoC was withdrawn in 2022 and `interest-cohort` has not been a real Permissions-Policy feature for years. Browsers ignore the unknown token (with a console warning), so it is harmless — but it is a 2021 copy-paste in a document that otherwise claims to be current, and it is the kind of thing a security reviewer uses to calibrate how much of the rest was verified.
fatal_flaws.correction: Drop it. If you want the useful modern additions, `browsing-topics=()` is the actual successor opt-out, and `Permissions-Policy: fullscreen=(self)` matters more for a video-hero product.

missing: Anthropic organisation rate limits. The entire funnel is denominated in dollars and never in RPM/ITPM/OTPM. A burst of queued generations at 32–128k output tokens will hit the org's output-tokens-per-minute limit and 429 long before the $500/day cap binds, and there is no backoff, no queue-depth-aware pacing, and no mention that Priority Tier is not available on claude-opus-5. The `attempts <= 2` ceiling turns a rate-limit blip into permanently failed customer onboardings.

Platform abuse and shared-fate blocklisting. Nothing in the document addresses the obvious use of a free AI site generator: generating phishing and scam pages on `<slug>.mijnsaas.com`. Because every tenant shares one registrable domain, one Google Safe Browsing / Microsoft SmartScreen listing of `mijnsaas.com` takes down all 10,000 tenant sites and your marketing site simultaneously. There is no content-abuse classifier on generated output, no takedown workflow, no `abuse@` handling, no phishing-term denylist on slugs and business names, and no plan for the separate tenant domain that would contain the blast radius.

Email as the single point of total compromise. Magic link is the only authentication factor at first login, and the site-claim token arrives the same way. Mailbox compromise, a mail-provider breach, or a subdomain-takeover of the sending domain is full account takeover for every user. No SPF/DKIM/DMARC (`p=reject`) policy, no BIMI/alignment story, no bounce/complaint handling, and no rate limit on sending claim invitations to *third-party* addresses the attacker types into the modal — which is both a spam-amplification vector and a reputation risk for your sending domain.

Observability PII. Workers Logs, Tail Workers, and Logpush are never mentioned. Prompts, business descriptions, lead form bodies, emails and phone numbers will flow through `console.log` and into log sinks by default, outside the EU jurisdiction guarantees the design makes for D1/R2. There is no log-redaction middleware, no sampling policy, and no statement of where logs are stored — while the privacy policy the product auto-generates will claim EU residency.

Backup, restore and destructive-action recovery. D1 Time Travel and R2 object versioning are not mentioned once. There is no answer to: a bad migration, a compromised deploy token running `DELETE FROM sites`, or a bug in the §8.5 cron that hard-deletes 'unclaimed after 30 days' sites. The retention crons are described as enforcement mechanisms with no dry-run mode, no soft-delete grace on the *site* itself, and no restore runbook.

Deploy-path and supply-chain security. gitleaks and push protection cover committed secrets, but nothing covers: the Cloudflare API token used by CI (scope, rotation, whether it can create Workers), account 2FA/SSO enforcement, npm dependency pinning and lockfile audit for a package set that includes `stripe`, `aws4fetch`, `@simplewebauthn/server` and the Anthropic SDK, or review requirements on the renderer and the HTMLRewriter gate — the two files where a single-line change silently disables the XSS boundary.

D1 sharding and multi-tenant isolation testing. §3.1 correctly names the membership-join invariant and says to enforce it as a lint rule and a test, but no such test is specified, and the invariant is stated for the dashboard only — `worker-sites`, the lead endpoint, the media resolver and the editor PATCH path each need their own tenant-scoping proof. Combined with the unaddressed 10 GB D1 cap, this is the pair of decisions most likely to require a rewrite at 10,000 tenants.

GDPR operational reality beyond the data map. No Art. 33 breach-notification runbook (72 hours), no Records of Processing Activities, no DSAR handling for *lead* data where you are processor and the tenant is controller (a visitor's erasure request arrives at the small business, who has no tooling — you must build it), and no answer for what happens to a tenant's leads when they cancel. The §8.5 export/erasure endpoints cover your own customers only.

Lighthouse feasibility. The document asserts the ~100/100 target is preserved by using CSP hashes for inline critical CSS, and never reconciles that with the product's mandated full-screen hero video plus a Cloudflare Stream iframe player. Stream's embed is a third-party iframe with its own JS payload; an autoplaying full-screen video is the LCP element on mobile. 100/100 mobile Performance with that combination will not survive an audit. If the video hero is non-negotiable, the honest answer is a poster-image LCP with the video attached after `load`, self-hosted as a short muted MP4 from `cdn.` rather than through Stream — which then changes the §5.7 CSP and removes the Stream cost line entirely.

Cost controls on the two *other* metered products the design introduces. §2.1 states the Anthropic bill is 'the single largest financial risk in the product' and builds six layers around it, then §4.2 mandates Cloudflare Stream (storage $5/1,000 min prepaid, delivery $1/1,000 min post-paid, billed per minute *delivered*) and Cloudflare Images ($0.50/1,000 unique transformations) with no cap, no per-tenant quota, and no budget DO. Stream delivery is the dangerous one: it is unbounded, driven by third-party traffic you do not control, and a single scraped or viral tenant page can generate four-figure delivery bills against €8.25/month of ARPU. There is no bandwidth alerting, no per-site delivery cap, and no kill switch.
verdict: The security *architecture* is genuinely strong and I would build on most of it — but three of its load-bearing implementation claims are wrong in ways that break the happy path before an attacker shows up, and one puts attacker-influenced HTML on the cookie origin. What is right is right for the right reasons: the origin split (static `www`, single-origin `app`, no CORS on the authenticated surface) is the correct foundation; opaque tokens hashed in D1 rather than JWTs, `__Host-` prefixes everywhere, atomic single-use consume via `meta.changes`, session rotation on claim, and the rule that a site is never claimable by slug or preview token together make the claim flow one of the better designs of its kind I have reviewed. The upload pipeline's core insight — presign into a *separate quarantine bucket*, derive the key server-side, mandatory re-encode, hard-deny SVG, serve from a cookieless `cdn.` origin with forced Content-Type and `default-src 'none'; sandbox` — is exactly right, and re-encode-as-sanitiser is the correct call for a platform that cannot run an AV engine. The Stripe section is better than most production code: raw body first, `constructEventAsync` with the SubtleCrypto provider, `livemode` checked against the environment, insert-before-process, and above all re-reading the object from the API instead of trusting event ordering, with the entitlement written in the same `batch()`. The card-fingerprint check for trial abuse is the actual answer to 'new email, same card'. Generating JSON-LD from D1 rather than from the model, and building `tel:`/`wa.me` links from the CHECK-constrained column, both close bypasses that most builders miss. The rate-limiting comparison table is accurate — I verified the 10-or-60-second period restriction and the per-Cloudflare-location semantics, the `[[ratelimits]]` GA config shape in §10 delta 1 is correct, and the §2.1 cost arithmetic checks out exactly against claude-opus-5 at $5/$25 per MTok with 0.1× cache reads. Now the problems. §5.4's schema regexes do not do what the document says they do: Anthropic structured outputs support `enum`/`const`/`anyOf` but not `pattern` or `maxLength`, and the TS SDK strips unsupported constraints and validates client-side — so the lowercase-only hex regex and the 600-char caps are not constraining the model, they are a client-side assertion that fails *after* you have paid for the call. `max_tokens: 32000` sits 40% below the document's own 45k typical-output estimate for a 36-page tree, so the flagship path truncates and fails to parse. The 180-second abort will kill successful generations mid-stream and hand them to Queue retry, double-billing the one thing the entire funnel exists to protect. Serving unclaimed sites from `app.mijnsaas.com/preview/<token>` contradicts both the document's own app-CSP (which allowlists a `preview.mijnsaas.com` that is never created) and its own iframe-isolation rule, and places pre-gate generated HTML on the origin holding every session cookie. And HEIC — the iPhone camera default, for an audience defined as small business owners uploading phone photos — requires an Enterprise Images plan to ingest, which breaks the mandatory re-encode step for the single most common upload. Add the wrong R2 endpoint host for EU-jurisdiction buckets, DOs with no jurisdiction pinned while the privacy policy claims EU residency, a tenant CSP that blocks the Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon the design elsewhere recommends, Turnstile hostname caps that make the lead-form story collapse at custom-domain scale, and D1's unraisable 10 GB cap with no sharding plan behind an immutable jurisdiction setting — and you have roughly two weeks of correction work, most of it cheap if done before the first `wrangler d1 create` and the first `Set-Cookie`. Do that work first: the jurisdiction flags, the shard key, the preview origin, and the passkey rpID are all one-way doors that are trivial today and expensive in six months. Sound enough to build on, not sound enough to build from as written.
